2047.description: BRIC-Opti was designed to provide a closed environment with an atmosphere of known initial composition for microbial growth in space. It provides a redundant level of containment for potentially hazardous materials, with autonomous logging of temperature data in three physical locations within each canister. Each BRIC-Opti contains four commercial OptiCells™ from BioCrystal, Ltd. BRIC-Opti was only flown once, to the ISS in 2006-2007, for the Passive Observatories for Experimental Microbial Systems in Microgravity (POEMS) experiment. POEMS was designed to evaluate the effect of stress in the space environment on the generation of genetic variation within model microbial cells. This experiment uses a new system for microbial cultivation in the spaceflight environment to observe the generation and maintenance of genetic variation within microbial populations in microgravity. POEMS will contain experiments studying the growth, ecology and performance of diverse assemblages of microorganisms in space. Understanding microbial growth and ecology in a space environment is important for maintaining human health and bioregenerative life support functions in support of NASA Exploration Systems requiring Advanced Life Support.

2048.description: The Plant Experiment Unit (PEU) is used within the Cell Biology Experiment Facility (CBEF) for plant life-science experiments on the International Space Station (ISS). The 1 g compartment has a centrifuge that can generate artificial gravity from 0.1 to 2.0 g. Experiment units (such as the PEU) are set in containment canisters and installed in the CBEF. The CBEF can control temperature (15-40°C), humidity (20-80%), and CO2 concentration. The PEU enables plant growth experiments from seed to seed and includes the following components: a plant growth container, a water delivery control system, an air ventilation control system, an illumination system (LED), a CCD camera, a temperature sensor, and a humidity sensor. Researchers can monitor operational data such as temperature, humidity, and water content of the plant bed, and observe real-time images of the growing plant. 21.description: The Drosophila Experiment Package consists of eight insect modules assembled into a two-tiered container. 24.description:
The Lysogenic Bacteria Experiment Packages are designed to grow replicate 1.2 ml cultures of two strains of lysogenic bacteria (Escherichia coli and Salmonella typhimurium P-22), without radiation and irradiated at three dose levels of gamma from 85Sr.  Sets of four special packages include a total of 96 bacteria growth chambers.  Three contoured packages of sixteen chambers, 1.2-1.8 ml each, receive, respectively, mean total dose exposures of 265, 645, and 1,630 r.  A fourth package of 48 chambers, 1.2 ml each, is for nonirradiated chambers.  The packages are fabricated to conform to isodose lines at an appropriate distance from the point 85Sr source.  The chambers are sealed with nylon machine screws and silicone O-rings. 

For loading, a single clone of each bacteria is grown overnight, and the resulting cultures are diluted to a final concentration of 120 cells/ml for S. typhimurium and 187 cells/ml for E. coli.  Cultures are maintained in suspension in spinner flasks over ice throughout loading into experiment packages, in order to impose a two-hour lag time prior to the start of cell growth.  S. typhimurium cultures are loaded into the top series of chambers, and E. coli are loaded into the chambers on the lower side of the package.  Samples are made at the start and completion of loading procedures to confirm that no growth has occurred.  Packages are kept on ice until mated with the spacecraft.  LiF dosimeters are included in each package.

components.description: The time between the loading of biological samples into the Shuttle and the activation of the experiment by the crew requires special equipment to maintain certain temperatures. Passive Thermal Conditioning Units (PTCUs) are storage containers for Biorack experiments, which fit into a middeck locker and can maintain a predetermined temperature over a twelve-day period. The PTCUs harness the latent heat capacity at the melting point of selected waxes and insulate the wax from the warm environment by double, stainless steel Dewar vessels. To improve thermal insulation before the samples are loaded, the volume between the double walls of the Dewar vessels is increased by vacuum pump up to 10-9 Torr. The vessels are also heated to 130 °C to remove any water vapor. A rack for 16 Biorack Type I and one Type II experiment containers, or 20 Type I containers alone, can fit inside a PTCU. The PTCUs fit into an aluminum case called the Middeck Locker Stowage Insert (MLSI).

components.description:
Each ATCU contains a cooler/freezer, incubators, and a glovebox.

Cooler/Freezer
The cooler/freezer is a combined unit that allows the maintenance of biological samples at temperatures that inhibit their metabolism. The cooler is capable of maintaining samples just above the freezing point (4 degrees Celsius). The freezer section can conserve samples at temperatures as low as -15 °C.

Incubators
The ATCU has two incubators that can be set accurately between 18 and 40 °C. Two centrifuges are included in each incubator to simulate a 1-g environment. Control samples, identical to those being exposed to microgravity conditions, are placed in these centrifuges. Comparing these two sets of samples, after their processing in the incubator has finished, permits the microgravity and radiation-environment effects to be identified.

Glovebox
The glovebox is a small working area for handling and observing biological specimens. The observations can be made through a microscope that is connected to photo, film, or TV cameras.
components.name: Active Thermally Controlled Units (ATCU)

components.description: To accommodate the number of items required to accomplish mission activities, the Biorack has stowage facilities.
components.name: Stowage

components.description:
Experiment hardware must fit in one of two types of sealed, anodized aluminum containers. Type I containers measure 90x58x24 mm, and Type II containers measure 79x79x99 mm. Each type of container can be connected electrically to the Biorack and are thus named Type I/E and Type II/E. Likewise, non-electrified containers are named Type I/O and Type II/O.

The electrified containers receive power by means of three electrical lines at +10, +5, and –10 volts and send data to the ground via, for Type I containers, two data channels and for Type II containers, four data channels.
components.name: Aluminum Containers

240.description:
Biorack is a reusable, multi-user facility developed by the European Space Agency (ESA) for studying the effects of microgravity and radiation on cellular functions and developmental processes in plants, tissues, cells, bacteria, and small invertebrates. The facility is equipped with a cooler/freezer, two incubators, and a glovebox. Experiment hardware must fit in one of two types of sealed, anodized aluminum containers. Type I containers are 90x58x24 mm and Type II containers are 79x79x99 mm.

The main parts of the Biorack are the Active Thermally Controlled Units (ATCUs), the Passive Thermal Conditioning Units (PTCUs), Stowage, and Aluminum Containers.

hardware_version.versionDescription:
The Biorack on IML-1 flew with one cooler/freezer; two incubators; a glovebox; stowage; aluminum containers for experiment-specific hardware; and five PTCUs: one at +10 degrees Celsius, three at +5 degrees Celsius, and one at –10 degrees Celsius.

US-1 (IML-1 and STS-76) Configuration:
Biorack on STS-76 contained two incubators and a glovebox, but no active cooling device. One incubator was maintained at 22 °C and the other at 36.5 °C. The incubators each contained new, variable-speed centrifuges, different from those that flew on IML-1. The new centrifuges were equipped with brushless d.c. motors and new control electronics. They could run at any one of three, pre-set, rotational speeds, resulting in three different levels of acceleration force.

The Biorack also contained three PTCUs: two at 5 °C and one at -10 °C.

On IML-1 and STS-76, the experiment made use of the following supplementary hardware which was stored in both Type I and Type II aluminum containers within the Biorack facility.

Lexan Tubes: Lexan polycarbonate tubes were assembled in four- and eight-tube configurations in Type I containers to maintain the nematodes in liquid buffered saline. The containers featured CR-39 film to document the tracks made by the radiation, kimfoil sheets to keep the film oxygenated, and thermal luminescence detection packages to measure radiation received.

Radiation Cartridge Belt: The belt, made of Nomex fabric with Pyrell foam-lined pockets and Velcro attachments, as attached to the Spacelab tunnel to absorb radiation. It held five Type I containers and one European Space Agency (ESA) temperature recorder.

Nematode Stack Assembly: Twenty-eight layered assemblies were contained within each Type II container. These assemblies consisted of a base support, worm/agarose layers on millipore filter paper, CR-39 film to track the path of radiation, kimfoil sheets, and Teflon sheets to act as a non-stick surface and to prevent dislodging the worm/agarose layer postflight when removing the CR-39 film.

For reflight on STS-76, major modifications were made to the experiment-specific hardware. For IML-1, the experiment was passive, with no crew activation of the experiment. For STS-76, a crew member initiated the experiment by injecting the nematodes into special lexan tubes. The tubes used to hold the worm cultures until injection into other exposure tubes were similar to those used on IML-1, but one end had a special cap designed for use with a syringe. The exposure tubes for STS-76 were of the same material but shorter and were housed in pairs inside an elemental tin shield. This shielding added weight to each container. A control exposure tube without radioisotopes was placed into an aluminum sleeve next to the tin-shielded tubes. The radiation cartridge belts were also different; for STS-76 they held aluminum canisters with syringes, whereas for IML-1 they held Biorack Type I containers.

The Biorack on IML-1 flew with one cooler/freezer; two incubators; a glovebox; stowage; aluminum containers for experiment-specific hardware; and five PTCUs: one at +10 degrees Celsius, three at +5 degrees Celsius, and one at –10 degrees Celsius.

US-2 (IML-1) Configuration:
The experiment also had its own supplementary hardware which was stored in Biorack Type I/O aluminum containers within the Biorack facility.

US 2 Cell Chambers: Each double chamber had two culture wells consisting of a Lexan chamber fitted with a movable piston and a molecular layer of silicone to ease piston travel. The yeast plate had two grooved areas into which Lexan rings fit. Prior to fixation, the piston was pushed down to vent the air inside the chamber. Fixative was injected through the piston with a hypodermic syringe.

US 2 Culture Assemblies: Four of the double chambers (a total of eight culture wells) were placed into a tray and inserted into Type I/O containers. The tray holding the chambers was fitted with a pad to ensure that the chambers were held adequately in place. These containers are opened only inside the Biorack glove box.

US-2 (STS-76, STS-81, STS-84) Configuration:
Biorack on STS-76 contained two incubators and a glovebox, but no active cooling device. One incubator was maintained at 22 °C and the other at 36.5 °C. The incubators each contained new, variable-speed centrifuges, different from those that flew on IML-1. The new centrifuges were equipped with brushless d.c. motors and new control electronics. They could run at any one of three, pre-set, rotational speeds, resulting in three different levels of acceleration force.

On STS-76 the Biorack also contained three PTCUs: two at 5 °C and one at -10 °C.

On STS-81 and STS-84 the Biorack contained two PTCUs at 5 °C.

The experiment also had its own supplementary hardware which was stored in Biorack Type I aluminum containers within the Biorack facility.

Plunger Box: The plunger box is a sterile environment for activating cell growth and fixating cells in microgravity. The box is composed of two culture chambers, each of which holds two 11x22 mm glass cover slips. The chambers are connected to three cylindrical compartments filled with media or fixative. The medium is forced into the culture chamber by manually releasing a spring-loaded plunger. The sealed plunger boxes allow astronauts to activate and inactivate cell growth in space flight and to store the samples for later analysis on Earth.

The Biorack on IML-1 flew with one cooler/freezer; two incubators; a glovebox; stowage; aluminum containers for experiment-specific hardware; and five PTCUs: one at 10 °C, three at 5 °C, and one at -10 °C.

US-3 (IML-1) Configuration:
The experiment also had its own supplementary hardware which was stored in Biorack Type I aluminum containers within the Biorack facility.

US-3 Cell Chambers: Limb bud cell cultures were contained in a Lexan polycarbonate chamber with two wells. Each well had a "bubble" of a gas-changing material, which expanded or collapsed as medium was added or removed. A silicon rubber gasket and bottom plate completed the basic assembly. Cells were cultured on coverslips inserted between the gasket and bottom plate. A deflector ring in the bottom of the chamber prevented fluid forces—produced during the medium injection and withdrawal—from dislodging or shearing the cells on the coverslip.

US-3 Chamber Assemblies: Four culture chambers (eight chamber wells) were inverted and placed on a tray designed to fit into a Type I container, thus allowing the four culture chambers to be removed as a unit. The chamber units were held in place in the tray by double-sided, sticky-backed tape. The medium exchange and fixation were performed by inserting a hypodermic needle through the gasket and onto the cultures on the cover slip.

Syringe Racks: The syringe racks held the syringes used to perform medium exchange and fixation of the cell cultures. The racks, made of Lexan polycarbonate, were designed in three different arrangements such that each one fit into a different location: the middeck locker stowage insert, the cooler, or the freezer. The cooler rack held 40 syringes filled with replacement medium. The stowage rack held the replacement-medium syringes that were transferred from the cooler rack following the Biorack's activation. Finally, the freezer rack stored syringes that contain removed, conditioned medium.

US-3 (STS-76) Configuration:
Biorack on STS-76 contained two incubators and a glovebox, but no active cooling device. One incubator was maintained at 22 °C and the other at 36.5 °C. The incubators each contained new, variable-speed centrifuges, different from those that flew on IML-1. The new centrifuges were equipped with brushless d.c. motors and new control electronics. They could run at any one of three, pre-set, rotational speeds, resulting in three different levels of acceleration force.

The Biorack also contained three PTCUs: two at 5 °C and one at -10 °C.

The experiment also had its own supplementary hardware which was stored in Biorack Type I aluminum containers within the Biorack facility.

US-3 Cell Activation Kit-1 (Cytokines): The kit consists of polycarbonate blocks or "cassettes," each stored in a Type I container. Each cassette is made up of six independent culture chambers and associated daughter chambers. The chambers can be manipulated by turning vanes to connect or to isolate them from each other or by pushing pistons to displace fluid from chamber to chamber. Activators can be added and supernatant filtered from cells by means of a filtering system within the cassette. After filtration, cells can be resuspended into the cassette using a multi-injector unit.

Biorack on STS-81 contained two incubators and a glovebox, but no active cooling device. One incubator was maintained at 22 °C and the other at 36.5 °C. The incubators each contained new, variable-speed centrifuges, different from those that flew on IML-1. The new centrifuges were equipped with brushless d.c. motors and new control electronics. They could run at any one of three, pre-set, rotational speeds, resulting in three different levels of acceleration force.

The Biorack also contained two PTCUs at 5 °C.

The experiment also had its own supplementary hardware which was stored in Biorack Type I aluminum containers within the Biorack facility.

44-US Cell Activation Kit-2 (Phorbal)
The kit consists of polycarbonate blocks or "cassettes," each stored in a Type I container. Each cassette contains six sets of three interconnected chambers. The largest of each set of three interconnected chambers includes a polished stainless steel plunger that acts as the test substratum for biofilm formation. The chambers can be manipulated by turning valves to allow mixing of bacterial suspensions with nutrient solutions and fixatives. Both activators and fixatives can be injected into each culture chamber. This kit does not have filtering capabilities.

Biorack on STS-81 and STS-84 contained two incubators and a glovebox, but no active cooling device. One incubator was maintained at 22 °C and the other at 36.5 °C. The incubators each contained new, variable-speed centrifuges, different from those that flew on IML-1. The new centrifuges were equipped with brushless d.c. motors and new control electronics. They could run at any one of three, pre-set, rotational speeds, resulting in three different levels of acceleration force.

The Biorack also contained two PTCUs at +5 °C.

The experiment also had its own supplementary hardware which was stored in Biorack Type I aluminum containers within the Biorack facility.

57-US Cell Activation Kit-2 (Phorbal)
Each cassette contained six sets of three chambers: a sperm chamber, a culture chamber, and a fixation chamber.

The sperm chamber and fixation chambers can each be connected to the culture chamber by turning the sluices that open independent channels between them. After opening the sperm sluice, a six-pronged activation tool simultaneously presses the plungers of the six sperm chambers, thus injecting the sperm into the six culture chambers containing sperm-activating buffer. The sperm sluice is then closed and the fixation sluice is opened. After 30 or 60 seconds of activation, the fixation plungers are then pressed thereby injecting the fixative into the culture chamber and thus terminating motility and phosphorylation.

Biorack on STS-81 and STS-84 contained two incubators and a glovebox, but no active cooling device. One incubator was maintained at 22 °C and the other at 36.5 °C. The incubators each contained new, variable-speed centrifuges, different from those that flew on IML-1. The new centrifuges were equipped with brushless d.c. motors and new control electronics. They could run at any one of three pre-set rotational speeds, resulting in three different levels of acceleration force.

The Biorack also contained two PTCUs at 5 °C.

The experiment also had its own supplementary hardware which was used within the Biorack facility for the Preplastid experiment.

Customized Type I and Type II Containers
Standard Biorack Type I containers (with drilled ventilation holes) housed the units for plant growth while the Type II container had a fixation device. Collectively, the internal components of the Type I and II containers were referred to as "lentil-roots" hardware.

In order to accommodate the small Arabidopsis seeds, the internal configuration of the mini-containers was modified by affixing seeds to a sandwich structure made of filter paper and membranes held together by neoprene O-rings. A sterile, gridded, black membrane of cellulose nitrate was placed on top of two layers of sterile paper. The mini-containers were cleaned and sterilized in 70 % (v/v) isopropanol, and subsequent steps were performed under aseptic conditions. Each side of the mini-container had 12 to 14 Arabidopsis seeds affixed to the membrane with one percent (v/v) gum guar. In some cases, twice as many seeds were sown per side of the mini-container.

Illumination Box
Although these experiments were conducted with dark-grown seedlings, the Arabidopsis seeds have a light requirement for germination. Two different types of illumination were used: light from the Biorack's glovebox and light from an illumination box.

For STS-81, illumination was provided by means of the Biorack glove box. This supplied illumination of 3.2 to 5.2 µM/m2s for a duration of 14h.

For STS-84, illumination was provided by means of an illumination box fitted with arrays of red light emitting diodes LEDs. The LEDs emitted light at 660 nm wavelength and the fluence rate at the level of the seeds was 130 to 170 µM/m2s with an illumination period of 10 min.

Biorack on STS-81 and STS-84 contained two incubators and a glovebox, but no active cooling device. One incubator was maintained at 22 degrees Celsius and the other at 36.5 degrees Celsius. The incubators each contained new, variable-speed centrifuges, different from those that flew on IML-1. The new centrifuges were equipped with brushless d.c. motors and new control electronics. They could run at any one of three, pre-set, rotational speeds, resulting in three different levels of acceleration force.

The Biorack also contained two PTCUs at +5 degrees.

The experiment also had its own supplementary hardware which was stored in Biorack Type I or Type II aluminum containers within the Biorack facility.

Cell Culture Units
The cell culture units (CCUs) fit into Type I Biorack containers and contain ten individual cell culture chambers, each capable of holding 0.9 ml of cells.

Medium Exchangers
Medium exchangers fit in the Type II containers and contain ten cylinders each with a piston that can displace the contents of the chambers. The volume of each cylinder is approximately 2 ml.

components.description: The box can house four adult female frogs and is divided into two compartments, with each compartment accommodating two frogs. The frog comparatments are lined with a soft, absorbent material to prevent skin abrasion. Frogs are kept moist with Ringer's solution, a solution of chlorides of sodium, potassium, and calcium, that is isotonic to animal tissue. The frog box slides into the FEU and mates with an air supply via quick disconnects. An aquarium-style air pump provides ventilation.
components.name: Adult Frog Box/Frog Box Chamber

components.description: The Human Chorionic Gonadotrophin (HCG)/Sperm Kit contains separate syringes filled with HCG and Ringer's solution, and Sperm Packages for holding sperm suspension and whole frog testes. The Egg Chamber Operations Kit holds forceps and petri dishes for egg handling. Ringer's Kits contain separate syringes for Ringer's solution and a mixture of Ringer's and Ficoll. Fixation Kits contain separate syrings for two types of fixative: a dilute acetic acid/dichromate buffer and formaldehyde. The Fixed Egg Chamber Kits contain boxes for holding egg chambers after fixation, as well as extra syringes for fixation.
components.name: Kits

components.description: Egg chamber units consist of three Lexan pieces assembled to form an incubation chamber for the growing embryos. The eggs are placed on a stainless steel grid inside an egg basket and fitted onto the eyepiece unit. The eyepiece features a viewport for examining embryos using a microscope and video equipment. The chambers may be filled with Ringer's solution, and can accommodate injections of fixatives or other materials.
components.name: Egg Chamber Units (ECUs)

components.description: The Power Conditioning Unit (PCU) accepts power from the Spacelab and distributes it to the various FEU subsystems. The PCU controls and indicators provide for set-up, monitoring, and operation of the FEU.
components.name: Power and Control Systems

components.description: The centrifuge provides an artificial gravity force of 1 g for onboard egg chambers. It has a double row of slots, color-coded to match the egg chambers.
components.name: Centrifuge

241.description: The Frog Environmental Unit (FEU) provides a ventilated and temperature-controlled habitat for four female frogs as well as groups of developing embryos. A centrifuge inside the FEU provides an artificial Earth 1 g environment, and can accommodate up to 28 Egg Chamber Units (ECUs). A separate compartment inside the FEU provides exposure to microgravity conditions for an additional 28 ECUs. Together, these systems offer the capability for simultaneous side-by-side experiments consisting of both a zero-g "treatment" group and a 1 g "control" group.

hardware_version.versionDescription: The hardware was flown on SL-J with all the components as described.

241.name: Frog Environmental Unit (FEU)

249.description: This NASDA provided hardware was used for cell culture.

hardware_version.versionDescription:
NASDA Life Science Cell Culture Kit (CCK) - Plant Fixation Chambers (PFCs) Configuration:

The Plant Fixation Chambers (PFCs) were provided by NASDA. They are aluminum, pertri-dish like containers which are approximately 100 mm in diameter by 35 mm high. Each chamber has a 15 mm septum port which extends 22 mm above the top of the container. These containers are completely sealed. The PFCs allow plant cells exposed to space flight to be fixed on orbit by insertion of a chemical fixative via syringe through the septum port. The fixative used was a 3% glutaraldehyde (balance water) solution. 20 ml of fixative was contained within each chamber.

249.name: NASDA Life Science Cell Culture Kit (CCK)

25.description:
The Neurospora (microorganism) Experiment Packages are designed to contain a large number of Neurospora conidia under conditions which prevent contamination and development of anoxia.  Conidia are deposited on moist Millipore filters held on polypropylene screens to maintain both sterility and high humidity.  A porous retaining ring is used to hold the Millipore filter in place on the screen and a polypropylene barrier is placed over the unit to contain each conidial sample within each disk.  The sample holders are stacked in groups of ten and held together and attached to the module cap with three screws.  The assembled module is screwed into a housing to complete the package assembly. The materials are autoclavable, biocompatible, and capable of causing minimal radiation shielding and backscattering.

Radiation Dosimeters
Three independent systems of thermoluminescent dosimetry are used:
     o  EG&G CaF2:Mn Mini thermoluminescent dosimeters
     o  EG&G LiF Mini thermoluminescent dosimeters
     o  Con-Rad LiF-Teflon disk dosimeters (5 mm thick)

hardware_version.versionDescription: The hardware was flown on Biosatellite II as described.

25.name: Neurospora (Microorganism) Experiment Package

26.description: The Pelomyxa (amoeba) experiment package consists of polycarbonate resin chambers divided into three 5 cc compartments, mounted inside a hollow box.  Each compartment is separated by Lexan pistons with ethylene propylene O-rings.  The first two compartments hold amoeba or paramecia that are mixed inflight via actuation of a Lexan shaft to which the pistons are attached.  Further actuation mixes the first two compartments with the third compartment which contains fixative.  Twenty-four chambers are mounted on five magnesium plates.  Front, back, and side magnesium covers are mounted on these plates.  The chamber shafts are spring loaded on one end and restrained by a multi-slotted face cam on the other end.  When the cam, which is rotated by a high-torque motor, moves from one position to the next, chamber shafts are pushed into the cam slots to achieve mix or fix chamber actuations.  These actuations, in turn, close micro-switches which serve as verifications of actuations.  Four of the chambers contain thermistors for measuring inflight temperatures.  These data are telemetered to the various ground stations.  High density foam pads are placed between chambers to damp vibrations during powered flight and re-entry.  The total package is bolted to the aft plate of the Biosatellite module.  A spacecraft timer initiates five inflight actuations.

hardware_version.versionDescription: The hardware was flown on Biosatellite II as described.

26.name: Pelomyxa (Amoeba) Experiment Package

components.description: These sensors are implanted in muscle tissue with short exteriorized leads.
components.name: EOG, EMG, EKG, ZPG

components.description: Signal conditioners for the low-level physiological outputs are located on the back of the animal's couch to minimize lengths of signal leads and provide practical interfaces for the animal/couch assembly with the rest of the flight system.  Each sensor (electrodes, thermistors, pressure transducers, etc.) converts the acquired physiological or environmental variable to an electrical analog.  This analog is conditioned (i.e. amplified, counted, etc.) to a voltage signal compatible with the telemetry system which then digitizes the data, codes it, and transmits it to the ground.
components.name: Signal Conditioners

components.description: The EEG electrodes, which collect ten individual measurements, are deep implants through the top of the skull, potted into a head cap of Kadon.
components.name: EEG

components.description: The brain temperature sensor is installed as part of the head cap assembly and is located in the posterior superior portion of the corpus collosum.  The body temperature sensor is attached to the urine catheter below the bladder.
components.name: Brain and Body Temperature

components.description: Blood pressure sensors are connected to the implanted catheters, which extend to four separate cardiovascular sites: the central artery; tibular artery, the pulmonary artery, and the central vein.  Two catheters are inserted into each leg near the medial surface of the knee and routed down each leg and covered with a nylon mesh "legging" before they connect to the fitting on the hammock.  This instrumentation is connected mechanically to the four teflon catheters that enter the body at the animal's thigh.  Pressures are measured at the transducer assembly, which is external to the animal.  A set of solenoid pumps inject a small volume of heparin into each catheter line at one-minute intervals to maintain the catheter tip (within the animal) clear of any clogging or clotting.
components.name: Blood Pressure Sensors

28.description: The primate onboard Biosatellite III is instrumented with physiological sensors including implanted electroencephalogram (EEG), electromyogram (EMG), electrooculogram (EOG), electrocardiogram (EKG), impedance pneumogram (ZPG), brain and body temperature electrodes, and blood pressure sensors. Transducers in the spacecraft measure capsule total pressure, partial pressures of oxygen and carbon dioxide, air temperature, pellet and water consumption, urine production, task performance, day/night light status, and any changes in capsule altitude. In total, there are 33 channels of physiological information (including urine data). Telemetry data and data from the onboard flight recorder and camera combine to form a uniquely complete record of the animal's health, environment, and behavioral responses in weightlessness.

hardware_version.versionDescription: The hardware was flown on Biosatellite II with all the components as described.

28.name: Primate Physiological Sensors

components.description: The psychomotor logic and control unit is a separate capsule component and contains the electronics for the psychomotor task operations and its associated data formatting.  This "housing" also has control interfaces with a number of spacecraft components within the capsule, such as the camera, tape recorder, and feeder.
components.name: Logic and Control Unit

components.description: In the VM task, two plastic disks lie one in front of the other and rotate in the same direction at approximately 85 revolutions per minute.  The front disk is transparent to permit the subject to track a button on the rear disk.  This button is exposed when the hole on the surface disk coincides with it.  The subject presses the button for correct response at coincidence.  Coincidence occurs approximately every two seconds during the trial.
components.name: Visuomotor (VM) Task

components.description: Twenty trials of delayed matching task are nominally followed by twenty trials of visuomotor task.  Nominally each trial lasts forty-five seconds.  Either task can be initiated or canceled by ground command.  Every correct response produces a brief flash of the secondary reward lamp, located near the psychomotor panel.  A food pellet can be obtained by operating the feeder lever arm after every second correct response.   A maximum of forty pellets per day can be obtained from successful task performance.
components.name: Behavioral Tasks

components.description: The psychomotor panel is positioned directly in front of the animal, positioned for easy reach and eye focus.  The apparatus consists of five switches and two overlapping revolving disks.  The panel displays the Nixie tube switches for the delayed matching task and the rotating concentric discs for the visuomotor task.
components.name: Panel

components.description: The five switches for use in the DM task are transparent windows with overlaying neon tubes capable of displaying symbols.  During each DM trial, the animal is required to respond by touching the center window display (A) within five seconds thereby extinguishing the display.  The symbol presented in the center display is selected randomly from a set of four (square, X, circle, triangle).  Approximately eighteen seconds later, the four symbols are displayed in a random pattern in the peripheral windows (B, C, D, E).  In a correct response, the subject touches the window displaying the symbol matching the just extinguished symbol of window A.  Incorrect choice or non-response to either presentation extinguishes the display and terminates the trial.
components.name: Delayed Matching (DM) Task

29.description: The Primate Psychomotor Test System consists of the display-response panel and the logic and control unit.  The system is designed to test the monkey in two behavioral tasks: one involves delayed matching of symbols for testing of recent memory and perception; the other tests coordination of eye and hand in detecting coincidence of two rapidly rotating objects.  Correct responses in either task arms the Pellet Feeder Dispenser with a food reward.

hardware_version.versionDescription: The hardware was flown on Biosatellite II with all the components as described.

29.name: Primate Psychomotor Test System

32.description:
The Radiation Source and Holder are designed to expose biological objects to a controlled amount of radiation inflight.

Radiation Source Capsule
The radioactive element, 85Sr powder, is poured into a stainless steel capsule.  Radioactive 85Sr is produced by irradiation enriched 84Sr(NO3)2 with neutrons. The resulting powder is then poured into a stainless steel capsule. The powder is retained within the capsule volume by welding the base plug in place. Only the portion above the plug contains the powder. After loading with powder, the radiation source capsule is then inserted into the Radiation Source Holder.

Radiation Holder
The purpose of the radiation source holder is to shield the radiation source before and after the exposure period and shield the control experimental packages in the aft section of the Biosatellite capsule.  It consists of an approximately hemispheric mass of sintered tungsten and associated drive mechanism.  A wheel is mounted in the holder.  A small section of the wheel projects above the top surface of the holder.  When the wheel turns, the source is retracted and the intensity at the surface of the holder will not exceed 40 mr/hour.  The drive mechanism, which rotates the source through the closed-open-closed cycle, is spring-driven with a solenoid-controlled latch mechanism.  As a backup safety measure, the source holder is designed to rotate to the safety position under the action of re-entry g forces, if the close command is not received.

hardware_version.versionDescription: The hardware was flown on Biosatellite II as described.

32.name: Radiation Source and Holder

33.description: The Rana (frog) experiment package consists of acrylic modules. Each module is divided into two chambers: 1) a 10-cc egg chamber and 2) a 4 cc fixative chamber. The O-ring-fitted piston separating the chambers is spring-loaded and actuated in module pairs, by preprogramming or by command. The actuation results in a forceful mixing of fixative and the egg medium.

hardware_version.versionDescription:
Gemini 8 and Gemini 12 Configuration:

Early versions of the hardware were utilized in frog egg experiments conducted on the Gemini-8 and Gemini-12 missions. They had four chambers each, each chamber capable of containing five frog eggs, for a total of 20. A partitioned section within each chamber contained a concentration of formalin, which when injected into the egg chamber gave a 0.5% concentration of formalin.  Packages were insulated and contained a temperature control system to maintain a temperature of 21 ±0.5 °C, and electrical power was obtained from the spacecraft.  The fixative injections were actuated by two handles on the outside of the package.

Biosatellite II Cofiguration:

The major innovation for Biosatellite I/II was the development of a treatment to detoxify the hardware plastics, principally outgassing by vacuum exposure, as well as a configuration appropriate to the Biosatellite environment, utilizing six times as many eggs.

For Biosatellite II, sixteen modules were inserted into a metal assembly which had external coils for the water-glycol coolant that maintains the experiment at 42.5 °F on the launch pad.  Four thermistors attached to each of four modules in the packages and provided a temperature readout.  A fifth thermistor served as a sensor for switching off strip heaters which were to raise the package temperature from 43 to 70 °F immediately postlaunch.  Thereafter, experiment temperature control was dependent on ambient spacecraft temperature.  Fertilized eggs were placed in groups of 10 in each of the first eight modules to be actuated, and in groups of five in each of the remaining.  Each one of the modules of a pair received the eggs from one of two donor frogs.  The glutaraldehyde fixative, in osmotically conditioned (sucrose) Sorensen phosphate buffer, yielded after mixing a final concentration of 2.5% glutaraldehyde.

33.name: Rana (Frog) Experiment Package

34.description:
The Tradescantia (flowering plant) experiment packages are constructed of polypropylene plastic to minimize absorption and scattering of the gamma rays from the onboard radiation source.  The packages are somewhat boomerang-shaped plastic housings 42 cm long, 4.7 cm wide, and 4.7 cm deep.  Each package holds 32 plants with the roots sealed in a tube filled with Hoagland's nutrient solution.  A comb-like retainer prevents the nutrient tubes from moving as a result of vibration, centrifugation, etc.  Tubes are stacked four deep and four across, for a total of sixteen tubes in each end of the polypropylene package.  When cuttings are placed in nutrient tubes, they form small, light, compact units suitable for use in the confines of a crowded Biosatellite.  Plastic fibers are placed around loose buds or stems during the loading process as shock-absorbing packing.  Small holes in the cover permit air exchange and some temperature control.  A thermistor is installed through the housing wall to monitor the package temperature.

Radiation Dosimeters
Numerous passive dosimeters of LiF powder are placed in the root and bud zones.  A dosimeter is placed into each of the nutrient tubes in the root zone.  For the bud zones, dosimeters are attached along the inside wall and on the retainer pins of the housing.

hardware_version.versionDescription: The hardware was flown on Biosatellite II as described.

34.name: Tradescantia (Flowering Plant) Experiment Package

35.description:
The Tribolium (flour beetle) experiment package consists of several plastic modules each with three compartments.  Each compartment contains an aluminum insert holding two felt layers sandwiched between tissue papers.  Holes are punched in each piece of felt, then one or two pupae are positioned in each hole in the felt inserts, cushioned between layers of tissue paper. The packages are constructed with integral heating strips and a preset thermostat; temperature control is automatic and required 28 V dc. There are two Tribolium packages, each of which contain 720 pupae.

Radiation Dosimeters
Four LiF disc dosimeters are inserted between two tissue papers with a pupae layer on either side then inserted into the plastic module.

hardware_version.versionDescription: The hardware was flown on Biosatellite II as described.

35.name: Tribolium (Flour Beetle) Experiment Package

36.description:
The Triticum (wheat seedling) experiment package consists of three cylindrical, nontoxic plastic chambers about 3 inches in diameter and 6.5 inches in height.  The chambers are fixed to a common base and are closed with individual lids with gaskets.  Each chamber has an insulating blanket to eliminate light and minimize heat loss.  Each chamber contains a seed-holding stalk place in its long axis, and a fourth, larger chamber contains three similar seed-holding stalks.  The polycarbonate plastic stalks are hollow with angled side arms set at spirally arranged at 120° so that each seed, when fixed, has the maximum amount of space in which to grow without its roots touching another seedling or the chamber wall.  The arms are set at 45° with one end of the central reservoir, a slurry of finely ground vermiculite and water in the interior of the hollow stalk.  Each chamber contains a thermistor for recording temperature.

Presoaked seeds are inserted into the rubber diaphragms of the stalks thoroughly wetted with ground vermiculite.  Each seed is inserted brush end first halfway through the hole burned in each cap, and then water is injected into the air spaces of the arm core.  Water loss is prevented by application of lanolin and beeswax (4:1 by weight) at the point of contact between the rubber diaphragm and the seed, after the seed is planted.  

The large chamber contains three polycarbonate stalks of twelve seeds each.  Of the three small chambers, two are equipped to spray-fix the fifteen seedlings during orbit.  Two cylinders, each with a capacity of 25 ml, are arranged to discharge their contents through nozzles in the floor of the chamber to which they are attached, so that a fine spray of fixative bathes the seedlings.  The firing of a squib activates a plunger which discharges the fixative at high pressure through the nozzles.

hardware_version.versionDescription: The hardware was flown on Biosatellite II as described.

36.name: Triticum (Wheat) Experiment Package

components.description: Each data collection period is initiated by a ground-based start pulse through the Biosatellite data system. Upon receipt of this start pulse, the internal time provided approximately twenty seconds each of high- and low-calibration signals followed by about 4.5 min of continuous, pulsatile data. At the end of the collection period, the controller disables power to the timer until receipt of the next start pulse.
components.name: Timer/Controller

components.description:
The flow and pressure transducers are contained within a single cylindrical molded cuff that is placed around the carotid artery of the Rhesus monkey during surgical implantation. The leads pass under the skin and exteriorize at the monkey's lower back. The cuff is constructed of injection-molded plastic to ensure that surfaces are smooth and that the upper and lower sections mate closely. The cuff consists of two parts: the top portion of the assembly which contains both pressure and flow transducers, and the lower portion which consists of several interchangeable shells capable of fitting around vessels ranging from 2.5-5.0 mm in diameter.

Sensors:
Pressure is measured using a 4.5 mm diameter and 1.2 mm thick titanium disk transducer capable of chronic implantation within the body. Pressure is sensed by imbalance of solid state strain gauge elements cemented to the inner, unexposed surface of the transducer diaphragm in a wheatstone bridge configuration. To improve longevity of the preparation and minimize damage to the vessel, the pressure cell is placed on the vessel's external surface rather than intravascularly.

Flow is measured using Doppler ultrasonic crystals and the continuous was technique. Crystals are positioned to lie on the leading edge of the cuff, proximal to the pressure transducer. The crystals are inserted at a compound angle, 45 degrees to the long axis of the vessel and 45 degrees towards its center. This placement of the crystals minimizes any turbulence effects from the decreased vessel cross section caused by the distally located pressure transducer.
components.name: Combined Pressure/ Flow (CPF) Cuff

components.description:
The U.S. signal conditioner accepts a "start pulse" from the Biosatellite on reaching orbit to become activated and also to transmit pressure and flow signals to the onboard Soviet tape recorder. Two cardiovascular signal conditioners are used: one measures pressure and flow from the CPF Cuff implanted in the primate; a second unit (along with a separate CPF Cuff) measures capsule ambient pressure to provide a correction and normalization for the implanted pressure sensor to 760 mm Hg. The outputs of each signal conditioner are recorded on separate, dedicated, on-board analog tape recorders.

Both reference and measured signals are conditioned for the 0-5 V input range of the onboard Soviet tape recorder. Electrical calibration values are 2 V for the high level and 0 V for the low level. These correspond to ideal physiological ranges of 0 to 200 mm Hg for pressure and a +/-1 KHz frequency shift for Doppler flow. The flow output signal is conditioned for an idealized physiological range of –1 KHz to +4 KHz frequency shift. The semiconductor strain gauge pressure cells are excited by a 5 mA constant current source. The output is conditioned for an idealized –200 mm Hg to +300 mm Hg physiological pressure range.
components.name: Signal Conditioners

components.description: The Barocel pressure sensor is an addition to the experiment hardware, flown earlier on Cosmos 1514, that measures ambient pressure throughout the mission. This is important because the vascular pressure is referenced to ambient pressure which can change frequently within the spacecraft. Barometric pressure is measured to correct and normalize the implanted pressure sensor to 790 mm Hg. No adjustments of the unit are possible. Power and signal conditioning are provided by an additional Signal Conditioner, with necessary modifications for processing ambient pressure data gathered on Cosmos 1667. Output of the sensor is adjusted for recording on the Soviet flight recorder. The 0.0 to 1,000 mm Hg range is equivalent to 0.0-5.0 V making output 0.5 V per 100 mm Hg. The device includes a highly accurate diaphragm capacitance transducer and is physically mounted in the spacecraft.
components.name: Ambient Pressure Sensor

37.description: Each cardiovascular monitoring system consists of a cuff for measuring pressure and flow, a signal conditioner, and a timer/controller apparatus.

hardware_version.versionDescription: The hardware was flown with all the components as described, except for the Ambient Pressure Sensor, as described.

Cosmos 1667 Configuration:

Modifications to the Cardiovascular Experiment Hardware included the addition of an Ambient Pressure Sensor and a highly specialized data handling system (PC-DARS) created to facilitate and allow for more accurate reporting of cardiovascular experiment data, following postflight transfer from the onboard Soviet tape recorder.  The Timer/Controller was combined in a single unit with the Signal Conditioners for the Ambient Pressure Sensor.

37.name: Cardiovascular Experiment Hardware

4.description:
The General Purpose Transfer Unit (GPTU) permits transfer of rodents in cages from the Research Animal Holding Facility (RAHF) to the General Purpose Work Station (GPWS). The GPTU has a Lexan frame with a sliding access door that interfaces with both the RAHF and the GPWS. A tyvek sock attached to the frame encloses the rodent cage during transfer. The GPTU is specifically designed to provide a second level of particulate containment.

The GPTU interfaces with the the Side Access Window (SAW) of the GPWS.  Two fasteners connect the two units and a tab on the GPTU sliding door fits into a slot in the SAW, allowing both doors to open simultaneously.

For interface with the RAHF, an adapter is required.  The adapter enables the GPTU to slide horizontally and vertically across the face of the RAHF to align with any rodent cage.  The GPTU has two fasteners that mate and align with dowels on the RAHF adapter.  A slight pressure is applied to compress the GPTU face gasket.  The fasteners are then turned to lock the two components together.  Releasing the fasteners allows the GPTU to slide to another designated cage location.

hardware_version.versionDescription: The hardware was flown on the Space Shuttle as described.
hardware_version.versionName: Version used on Space Shuttle Missions

4.name: General Purpose Transfer Unit (GPTU)

components.description:
Body temperature is obtained from a subcutaneous sensor developed by the Soviet research team for implantation in the axilla of the monkey.  It transmits a radio signal to a Soviet receiver every 16 minutes which provides a pulse train whose frequency is proportional to temperature (Soviet-provided table for °C/Hz).  An event-counting Solicorder unit is used to count the pulses and store a frequency in memory for later conversion to temperature data.  This recorder is modified for compatibility with the Soviet receiver signal characteristics.  Electrical isolation from the Soviet receiver is achieved with an optical coupling to avoid ground-loop problems.

Skin temperature is measured by a U.S.-developed thermistor attached to the monkey's ankle skin by cyanoacrylate glue, and then covered with tape.  The output of the thermistor is recorded on its dedicated temperature-reading Solicorder unit.

Activity is monitored using a U.S.-developed sensor attached to the monkey's restraint jacket and signal conditioner.  The activity sensing system required extensive testing with monkey subjects to determine the proper sensitivity setting and sensor location.  The output of the sensor is filtered and amplified, fed into its dedicated event-counter Solicorder unit and totaled over sixteen-minute intervals.
components.name: Sensors

components.description: To record ambient temperature inside the biosatellite, a U.S.-developed temperature recorder was planned for the flight.  Although an earlier version of the unit was successfully flown on Cosmos 1129, a last-minute requirement to test the function of the recorder at the launch site could not be fulfilled.  As a result the unit was not flown on Cosmos 1514.
components.name: Temperature Recording System

components.description: The Solicorder is a solid state, single-channel, digital recorder available either in temperature-reading or event-counting models.  Three Solicorder units were included in the flight package for Cosmos 1514.  Two event counter-type and one temperature-type recorders are combined into a single package for flight.  The flight package uses only the commercial circuit boards which were custom-manufactured to NASA standards.  Power is supplied by lithium batteries
components.name: Solicorder Flight Package

42.description: Three sensors (U.S. or Soviet) are used to measure skin temperature, body temperature, and motor activity.  These data are recorded to a U.S.-developed Solicorder Flight Package.

hardware_version.versionDescription: The hardware was flown on Cosmos 1514 with all the components as described.

42.name: Circadian Rhythm Experiment Hardware

49.description: The centrifuge was used on Cosmos 782 and Cosmos 936 to provide a source of artificial gravity aboard the spacecraft.

hardware_version.versionDescription:
Cosmos 782 Configuration:

For Cosmos 782 a centrifuge with fruit flies, fish embryos, and carrot tissue/cells, that could receive a force of 1-g or 0.6-g.  The upper platform of the biosatellite was a centrifuge that was set to rotate at a constant speed of 52 rpm.  Containers with fruit flies, Fundulus embryos, carrot tissue and cultured carrot cells were placed on this platform.  They received a 1-g or 0.6-g force, depending on their position on the centrifuge.  A stationary lower platform held materials identical to those on the upper platform.

Cosmos 936 Configuration:

For Cosmos 936, two groups of cages were placed on centrifuges. The cages on the centrifuges differed from the other rat cages only in direction of air flow.  In the centrifuged cages, air entered through holes in the cage doors rather than through the tops of the animal compartments.  Air was forced through the cages when the centrifuges rotated.  The centrifuges were activated at the time of spacecraft insertion into orbit and deactivated shortly before landing.  Rotation on the centrifuges provided an acceleration of 1-g to the ten rats housed in these cages.

49.name: Cosmos Centrifuge

components.description: The Thermal Control System controls air temperature inside the cabinet, which can be maintained between 20 and 29 degrees Celsius. Caution indicators are illuminated when the system fails to maintain the cabinet air temperature to within 2 degrees Celsius of a set point.
components.name: Thermal Control System

components.description: The rack-mounted, retractable cabinet provides laboratory work bench accommodations, including airflow, power, and lighting. The cabinet's front door allows large experimental hardware to be transferred inside during flight. Ports on the front and side of the cabinet allow two crew members to simultaneously perform tasks inside the cabinet using gauntlets. The entire cabinet may be locked into one of three extended positions during use or fully recessed into the rack for stowage. Waste may be deposited in a disposal compartment through rubber slits on the rear wall of the internal work volume.
components.name: Cabinet

components.description: The electrical system accepts AC/DC power from the Spacelab for experiment-related equipment. Panels on the front and inside the cabinet volume contain power switches and temperature controls.
components.name: Electrical System

components.description: The system is designed to clean the air within the work volume and provide biohazard protection. In includes a circulation blower, a main trace Contaminant Control System (TCCS) canister, a vent canister, High Efficiency Particulate Air (HEPA) filters, absorbent fiberglass blotter pads, and a manually operated Air Diverter Valve. The GPWS incorporates two modes of operation: normal for nominal operations, and recirculation to facilitate cleanup in the event that fluid and debris are released into the cabinet.
components.name: Containment Control System

5.description: The General Purpose Work Station (GPWS) is a multi-purpose support facility for conducting general laboratory operations within the Spacelab. The GPWS supports biological experiments, biosampling, microbiological experiments, and it serves as a closed environment for containment while routine equipment repair or other in-flight operations are performed. The GPWS provides the essential working space and accommodates the laboratory equipment and instruments required for many life sciences investigations. Housed in a Spacelab double rack, the GPWS is self-contained, apart from power, data, and cooling interfaces.

hardware_version.versionDescription:
Spacelab Life Sciences 1 (SLS-1) Configuration:

The hardware was flown on SLS-1 with all the components as described. Several additional hardware items were designed, in conjunction with the Particulate Containment Demonstration Test (PCDT) cage, to verify that the design of the General Purpose Work Station (GPWS) was adequate to contain particulates under a simulated 10-day mission of rodent waste materials. The PCDT GPWS items included the following articles:

Particle Dispensers: Particle Dispensers were operated manually in the GPWS. The particle dispenser was made up of a balloon pre-filled and attached to an inflation bulb. The balloon was inflated to approximately 6 inches in diameter by manually pumping the inflation bulb. The particle load was then dispensed within the GPWS by rupturing the balloon with a pin.

Fluid Dispenser: The Fluid Dispenser was a standard STS crew cup with a drinking straw as a nozzle. Each crew cup contained 120-150 ml of colored water with approximately 60 ml being dispensed per test. Wipes were used to detect any fluid leakage out the GPWS cabinet by showing a colored stain. The crew member inserted his/her hands inside the GPWS through the side port gauntlets and, using a second crew cup on top of the one containing the colored water, pressed down, releasing the colored water into the GPWS work space.

Volume Simulators: The volume simulators represented those that were used in the cardiovascular experiment on the SLS-2 flight. These simulators were for the microscope and flow meter (represented by a zero box containing the particle and fluid simulators). One of the PCDT cages was also placed inside the GPWS, creating a realistic profile in the GPWS by disrupting the cabinet airflow in a way that was representative of a flight configuration.
Film and crew voice recording, along with post flight analysis, determined the efficiency of the clean-up and GPWS containment design.

Spacelab Life Sciences 2 (SLS-2) Configuration:
 The GPWS was flown on SLS-2 with all of the components as described. When configured for the SLS-2 mission, the Side Access Window from the hardware's original design was reinstalled, but the added coolant line insulation was left intact.

Spacelab Japan (SL-J) Configuration:
 The hardware was flown on SL-J with all of the components as described. The hardware was further modified to meet experiment manipulation requirements. Specifically, the sliding Side Access Window was replaced by a solid lexan window. In addition, the lower temperature requirements of this payload required provision of additional coolant lines.

Neurolab Configuration:
 For Neurolab, minor modifications to the GPWS were made to accommodate integration of experiment specific hardware for the 9301100 and 9301150 experiments. Modifications included two video cameras mounted inside the GPWS to record activities for these experiments and an interface box mounted on the outside of the GPWS to provide power to the video cameras.

During flight, the Animal Walking Apparatus (AWA) for experiment 9301150 was deployed in the GPWS to conduct the experiment sessions.

5.name: General Purpose Work Station (GPWS)

50.description: The Soviets provided sheetmetal flight containers that housed standard, cotton-stoppered fruit fly vials with standard food medium for the fruit fly experiment.

hardware_version.versionDescription: The hardware was flown on Cosmos 782 and 936 as described.

50.name: Cosmos Fruit Fly Container

51.description: Fish embryos were housed inside a two-chambered aluminum case. Each chamber contained five flattened polyethylene bags separated by thin perforated foam. Embryos were suspended in artificial sea water inside the polyethylene bags. For flight on Cosmos 782, fish embryos were maintained in both a stationary location and on the onboard centrifuge.

hardware_version.versionDescription: The hardware was flown on Cosmos 782 as described.

51.name: Cosmos Fundulus Chambers

52.description: The Cosmos spacecraft contained two monkey BIOS capsules, which provided life support and experiment hardware. The orientation of the two capsules within the spacecraft allowed the monkeys to view each other. Monkeys were placed within restraint couches in each capsule. A remotely controlled chest restraint pad, a lap restraint plate with a leg divider, and upper and lower arm restraint straps were used to maintain each monkey in an appropriate, comfortable posture and to provide adequate support upon ground impact. The degree of thoracic restraint could be modified by ground command. Unidirectional air flow moved excreta toward a centrifugal collector underneath the restraint couch. The monkey could activate the paste diet and juice dispensers located in each capsule by operating bite switches. The monkey's access to these dispensers could also be controlled remotely from the ground. A camera mounted within each capsule monitored inflight animal behavior. A 16:8 light/dark cycle was provided in the monkey compartments during the flight. A psychomotor system within each capsule was used to test the responses of the monkey subjects to various stimuli. The monkeys were trained to press a lever whenever a light signal was presented. The strength required to press the lever could be determined from the EMG signals recorded from limb muscles. Vestibular tests conducted inflight included monitoring the eye-tracking response of the monkeys to a semi-circular array of programmed lights located in front of each monkey. A sensor attached to the skull cap of one monkey registered that a correct response had been made when the sensor was pointed directly at the light on the panel. Juice rewards were presented for correct responses. Vestibular tests also required subjecting the animals to a slow sinusoidal motion in the head-to-foot direction. This movement was produced by a motorized oscillator attached to the restraint couch.

hardware_version.versionDescription: The hardware was flown on Cosmos 1514, 1887 and 2044 as described.

52.name: Cosmos Primate-BIOS

53.description: Rodent cages on Cosmos 782, Cosmos 936 and Cosmos 1129 were provided by the U.S.S.R. Each cage consisted of two intercommunicating cylinders. Each had a diameter of about 9.5 cm and was about 20.8 cm long. The upper cylinder housed the rat, while the lower one served as a waste collection trap. Cabin air circulated through the cages and was returned, via the lower cylinder, to the cabin after being passed through an activated charcoal filter. The upper animal chamber was furnished with light on a 12:12 light:dark cycle. An automatic watering system provided water ad lib to the animal. A feeder cup dispensed ten grams of paste food every six hours. A circular coil surrounding the cage monitored physical activity. Cages were arranged in groups of five and a common food and water reservoir used for each group.

hardware_version.versionDescription: Rats were housed in individual cages on Cosmos 782, Cosmos 936 and Cosmos 1129. For Cosmos 936, two groups of cages were placed on centrifuges.

53.name: Cosmos Rodent Cages

54.description:
For rodent experiments on Cosmos 1514,  Cosmos 1887 and Cosmos 2044,  rats were group-housed in a single compartment called the Rodent-BIOS. The BIOS was formed by removing the partition that separated males and females in the Cosmos 1129 rodent mating chamber. It was equipped with ten nozzles for delivering paste food and ten nozzles for dispensing water. Food was provided at regular intervals; water was available ad lib to the animals. Unidirectional airflow moved wastes and debris into a waste collector located at the bottom of the cage. The light/dark cycle was regulated to 12:12.  

Ground support equipment for the rat neuroontogeny experiment included maternity cages with video monitors, rotation and tilt devices for vestibular tests and an olfactory, respiration, auditory and visual testing system.

hardware_version.versionDescription: The hardware was flown on Cosmos 1514, 1887 and 2044 as described.

54.name: Cosmos Rodent-BIOS

57.description: The Rodent Mating Chamber, developed by the USSR, was designed to support embryology experiments onboard the Russian Cosmos Biosatellite. The chamber accommodates seven rats and can be partitioned by a remotely activated door to separate male and female rats until the door should be opened to allow rats to mingle and possibly mate, upon wich the door can be opened. The chamber includes eight feeding stations, providing the animals food at regular intervals. Water is available to the rats ad libitum. Unidirectional airflow moves wastes and debris into a waste collector located at the bottom of the cage. The lighting system regulates the light/dark cycle.

hardware_version.versionDescription: The Rodent Mating Chamber was flown on Cosmos 1129 as described.

57.name: Rodent Mating Chamber

components.description:
The camera-mirror system automatically records rat behavior and general activity during the critical periods of launch, flight, and re-entry. The system consists of a 16 mm camera, a camera controller, and reflecting mirrors.

Camera: The camera is provided by Johnson Space Center. It has a shutter speed of 1/30 to 1/500 seconds at 6 frames per second. Time exposure is 2 to 48 frames per second with 6 frames per second being used on SL-3. The camera is equipped with a 25 mm lens and a film magazine with 400 feet of thin-based film. A film footage indicator, located on the magazine cover, reads FULL when the camera is loaded and EMPTY when all of the film has been exposed. The data annotation module on the camera's underside provides a time display directly on the film. The camera has three clock set switches: RESET, FAST, and SLOW, and an LED read-out.

Camera Controller: The camera controller contains the controls to preselect frame rate, run time, mode, and off time. Also, the power and run switches allow the system to operate and are guarded. At late access, when the animals are loaded into the RAHF, the camera control switches are set as follows.

MODE: ASC (ascent). On g-force activation, the mode is automatically switched to CONT (continuous). The camera is reset, as required by procedure, during the flight and is set to DSC (descent) at spacelab de-activation.
FRAME RATE: 6 frames per second
BURST TIME: 30 seconds
INTERVAL TIME: 7.5 minutes. 

The camera and its controller are secured to a bracket that is mounted on the upper front portion of the RAHF module. The camera and controller cover cages 1, 2, 3, and 4 when the devices are closed. The camera lens is directed at 8 reflecting mirrors that are mounted on the lower portion of the RAHF module. This allow cages 9, 10, 11, and 12 to be filmed (these cages do not have outer, light-shielding doors). The camera and controller are powered by means of a connection on the upper electronics box control panel. They are secured to the cage module by three thumbscrews and a hinged structure that allows them to "swing" away for changing the feeder and waste tray.
components.name: Camera System

components.description:
A 28 volt DC powered centrifugal blower is located below the cage module as a part the sub-system known as the Single Pass Auxiliary Fan (SPAF).  Its purpose is to increase the negative pressure system within the cage module whenever the feeder or waste tray doors are open and to cause any particulates to be drawn into the module.  Two holes are cut into the bottom of the cage module where a manifold is attached.  A coarse screen filter and a sliding gate valve are in the manifold.  The manifold is connected via hose to the SPAF blower.  A thermal  switch interrupts power if the temperature on the hottest part of the motor casing exceeds 165 degrees F and resets at 155 degrees F.  SPAF discharge air is directed through a .3 micron filter before entering the Spacelab atmosphere via louvers on the bottom half of the SPAF front panel.  Provisions are made for aisleway ducting so one SPAF can service several RAHFs and a standby auxiliary SPAF is also available.

SPAF Operation:  When the SPAF power switch is placed in the on position, the bleed air fan switch is placed in the off position.  This turns the RAHF bleed air system off to prevent overheating the bleed fan motors.  The TEU and CIRC fan switches are also turned off during SPAF operation.  The gate valve controls a normally closed guillotine type shutoff valve that isolates the cage module from the SPAF and is pulled out to open the valve and allow SPAF air to penetrate the cage module.  An AUX DUCT port is available on the top right side to permit connecting a hose from the primary SPAF to an auxiliary unit located in an adjacent rack.
components.name: Single Pass Auxiliary Fan (SPAF)

components.description:
The side and rear walls of rodent cages are made from anodized aluminum. The cages have perforated metal floors and top doors to permit air circulation. The top of each cage is a lexan panel that contains a specific pattern of holes which equalize air flow within the various cages. The panels remain assigned to specific cage slot numbers to achieve this equalization.

The cages have a polycarbonate window that separates the front and the rear compartments. Individual rodents are housed in each compartment and a data connector is located in the rear. The data connector allows transmission of food, water, and activity count to the data system.

The tops of the cages are hinged to permit the crew access to the animals when the cage is removed from the module. For SL-3, the cages also had 2 holes to allow the animals access to the watering "lixits" installed in the plenum above the cages.

Each cage contains a spring-loaded feeder for each rat and a bottom waste tray to accumulate urine and feces. The waste tray is chemically treated to control odor and bacterial growth.

Like the primate cage, each rodent cage has two activity monitors that are infrared beams near the front and rear of the cage. Each time the animal breaks the beam, a signal is sent to the data system.

The cages are held in place at the rear by 2 tapered pins that mate with the cage module.

For SLS-1 and SLS-2, the rodent cage system was redesigned with a mesh screen as a partition between the front and rear compartments. The front doors of the cage were also redesigned and better gaskets were installed to improve particulate containment.
components.name: Rodent Cage

components.description: The system collects three types of data: 1) Temperature, humidity, water pressure and air pressure across the Environmental Control System fans (air flow) are collected as analog data; 2) Heating, cooling, lighting, and a drinking water out-of-limit condition are collected as discrete data; and 3) Water delivery and activity are collected as pulse-code modulated data. The data system collects selected data and sends it from the front panel of the RAHF to an umbilical for monitoring selected RAHF data prior to launch, and to a recorder during liftoff and landing; it formats data through a Remote Acquisition Unit (RAU) for processing by the onboard experiment computer utilizing a series of data display formats.
components.name: Data System

components.description:
The Inflight Refill Unit (IRU) can be used to transport water from the orbiter middeck galley to the RAHF when necessary. The IFU has two primary components.

Fluid Pumping Unit (FPU): The FPU includes a pump/motor, piping, sensors, and the supporting structure required for pumping water through the IRU hardware. The FPU's positive displacement pump contains an integral motor designed for continuous operation. A motor drive control governs pump speed by regulating the motor input voltage. A current limiting device is also provided. Power is not required when filling the system, but is required at the RAHF when transferring water to the water tank and when disposing of excess water. Two counters are provided that mechanically indicate the number of liters of water pumped (resettable) and total liters pumped (not resettable). The FPU is contained in a nomex cloth pouch for easy storage and transportation.

Collapsible Water Reservoir (CWR): The CWR, also contained within a nomex cloth, is a flexible, stowable bag that holds water to be transferred. The reservoir's body is constructed of two layers: An inner bladder of a polyether polyurethane material that is compatible with potable water and an outer bladder of Kevlar-reinforced urethane. This outer bladder holds pressure and protects against accidental cuts and tears. A panel of urethane is attached to both sides of the CWR to limit its expanded height. A thermoplastic hose with a quick-disconnect mates with the FPU.

The IRU also has an adapter that enables excess water to be dumped into the orbiter waste collection system by means of a quick-disconnect at the IRU and a twist lock connection to the waste system.

The IRU also has a tether to meet Shuttle safety requirements.
components.name: Inflight Refill Unit (IRU)

components.description: Rodent food is supplied ad libitum in the form of a compressed diet bar. Rodent food is molded in rectangular bars that mount in a spring-loaded, side-mounted bar feeder. The bars are driven against a stop in such a way that the food bar is advanced as the rat consumes food, triggering a microswitch and a counter that records the number of clicks and, therefore, the amount of food bar remaining. Food bars can be changed by crew members through the feeder cassette without removing animals from the cage.
components.name: Rodent Feeder

components.description:
The Primate Cage contains two windows—one solid and one perforated—one behind the other. The outside window, made from polycarbonate, allows crew members to view the animals. The perforated inner window allows limited access to the animal in the event that such access is required.

A lixit protruding from the cage's rear wall provides water. A pellet dispenser occupies the upper left side wall. The primates obtain a banana-flavored pellet from the dispenser by tapping a lever within the cage a set number of times. Whenever a pellet is dispensed, the count is recorded in the RAHF Data System.

The top of the cage is perforated sheet metal, which allows air ventilation. Waste products are carried through the floor to the attached waste tray, which is chemically treated to control odor and bacterial growth.

The cage has an activity monitoring system. It consists of two infrared beams, one located about a quarter of the distance from the front of the cage and the other located about a quarter of the distance from the rear of the cage. Each time the beam is broken, a count is sent to the data system.
components.name: Primate Cage

components.description: Each rodent and primate cage compartment contains one or more activity monitors that record general animal movement (one for each rodent cage, two for each primate cage). The monitor consists of an infrared light source (920 nm beam) and sensor mounted on the right side of the cage and reflector tape mounted on the left side of the cage. When the animal breaks the light beam and therefore the circuit, a counter is electronically advanced one pulse. The counter reading is recorded by the RAHF Data System for transmission to the ground in realtime or near realtime.
components.name: Activity Monitor

components.description:
The Environmental Control System mounts on the back of the cage modules and has 3 parts: the Air Circulation Component, the Thermoelectric (TEU) Component, and the Auxiliary Water Pump Component.

Air Circulation Component: Two propeller fans pull cabin air from the RAHF cage module and return a portion of the circulating air to the cabin through a filter and a charcoal bed, which removes odors and particulate matter. These two filters bacteriologically isolate the animals and crew, and ensure that the RAHF maintains a slightly negative pressure with respect to the cabin. Air within the RAHF is circulated by a cluster of four propeller fans.

For SLS-1 and SLS-2, the Environmental Control System was augmented with a Single Pass Auxiliary Fan (SPAF) to increase negative pressure in relation to cabin air, thus ensuring particulate containment within the RAHF during cage/animal operations. SPAF operation required adding a check valve at the charcoal bed output of the bleed air system to prevent back flow during SPAF operations. A modification at the bottom of the cage module was made to the air circulation system to permit connectivity of the SPAF to the internal air system. The SPAF is a 28-volt DC centrifugal blower that forces air through a manifold at the bottom of the cage module, through hoses, and is discharged to the cabin via a 3 micron filter. Discharge air enters the cabin via louvers on the bottom half of the SPAF front panel. Provisions are made for aisleway ducting so that one SPAF can service several RAHFs. A stand-by auxiliary SPAF is also available.

Thermoelectric (TEU) Component: This controls temperature by drawing a portion of the circulating air into the TEU's cold side. The air is drawn into the unit by means of a hydrophilic coating that condenses the air into water (for humidity control) by capillary action. This water, together with some air, is sucked from the trailing edge of the aircore and pumped by a water separator into a condensate collector bottle. The cold, dehumidified air is warmed, as necessary, by a heater and is remixed with circulating air prior to its return to the cages. A thermoswitch located on the TEU's inlet water heater shuts down the TEU in case of water loss and subsequent TEU overheating.

Auxiliary Water Pump: The RAHF is equipped with its own auxiliary water pump that is used when the Spacelab system is not operating.
components.name: Environmental Control System (ECS)

components.description:
Every cage has 2 lamps, each one providing 2.1 lumens or 5 foot candles of light at the cage's floor level. The lamps are long-life, incandescent types and are mounted in the air plenum above the cages. Cage illumination is provided on selectable day/night cycles and can be controlled either manually or automatically via an adjustable timer on the RAHF's control panel.

For the rodent cages on SL-3, the lighting for each of six tiers of drawers could be independently controlled manually or automatically. The automatic or timed operation is performed by setting the "on" and "off" time dials on the front of the RAHF rack.

For SLS-1 and SLS-2, the light cycle could be independently adjusted by cage "quadrants," four cages to a quadrant, also on the RAHF's control panel.
components.name: Lighting System

components.description:
The RAHF ad libitum watering system consists of a pressurized bladder tank, pressure regulator, and a system of 24 sets of solenoids, pressure switches, and accumulators that measure increments of water to lixit valves for the animals, and water consumption counters. The self-pressurized bladder tank is located in the uppermost part of the RAHF. As the water is used up, a diaphragm collapses the bladder; the expansion of a pressurized gas in the remainder of the tank ensures water pressure in the absence of gravity.
